How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

A conscious scene is experienced as one scene, although many brain regions contribute to it. We propose that this unity requires physically enforced agreement: the regions must be coupled so that any change in one, as long as it exceeds that region's own noise, reaches the others and pulls them back toward agreement within the time a percept takes to form. The condition is stricter than cause and effect, since the bits of a computer also act on one another, and it separates cortex from digital hardware at a finer functional grain than the algorithm. A machine-checked bound makes the digital side precise: under noise, content read from bits responds to a small physical change by at most the probability that a bit comes near its threshold, so bits read well clear of their thresholds fail the condition. Applied to model membranes fitted to recordings from awake mice, the same test finds that at least one of 10 independent carriers reaches a sensitive state within a percept's time with probability at least 0.91. The premise itself is an empirical hypothesis, and we propose an experiment to test it: reconnect two cortical regions through an analog or a quantized loop, vary bandwidth and quantization separately, and compare reports of unity with a rival model in which only bandwidth, delay and nonlinearity matter. The condition also predicts that cortical coupling restores agreement within 166 ms.

• Restoration: the coupling pulls overlapping contents back into agreement before those contents change.

Counting says what the physical whole is; restoration says which couplings keep its contents consistent. Together they motivate P. The formal results then show what follows: noise margins cap how much a record can respond, records drop out of the chains that counting builds, and graded readers can join regions. Whether experience tracks this condition is argued in Section 3, and tested in Section 6 through a stated link between experience and reports.

Noise and time. Two refinements make P applicable to noisy carriers. Physical systems are noisy, so P is read on probabilities: a change counts only if it is larger than the part's own noise, and it must then move what the part does next by at least as much as the part fluctuates by itself. And a neuron is sensitive to small inputs mainly when it is close to firing, so asking every neuron to be sensitive

1 Introduction

When you watch a bird fly across the sky, you see one bird in one scene. Yet many parts of your brain work on that scene at once. A visual area tracks where the bird is, and a parietal area tracks the same location to plan a reach toward it. Each part describes a piece of the same situation, and their descriptions agree. This paper asks what kind of agreement that has to be.

Parts can agree in two ways. Picture first a set of weights joined by springs. Each weight's position is a graded physical quantity that pulls on its neighbours all the time, so no weight can move, even slightly, without dragging the others after it. The weights are coordinates of one physical state, and above their own noise they cannot vary independently at any scale. We call this agreement physically enforced. Picture next a set of account books kept consistent by a clerk, who at fixed times compares the books and corrects any mismatch. Between checks a smudge on one page changes nothing in any other book. The books agree only because a rule makes them agree, and we call this agreement computed. The springs make one system in the sense physics uses; the books are many systems kept in step by a protocol. Both involve causes, of course: the clerk reads one book and writes in another. The difference is which changes get through. Any displacement of a weight changes the pull on its neighbours, whereas a smudge that leaves a numeral readable changes nothing the clerk does.

A digital chip is of the second kind. Each bit is a separate record, built to ignore small disturbances: a voltage a little above or below the level for 1 still reads as 1. That makes computers reliable, and it also seals each bit off from small changes in every other bit, so whatever agreement a program produces among its bits is computed. The line falls where the bits are read: a converter that samples a graded signal finer than its noise is judged by the same test, and can pass it. Our premise is that the unity of an experience is agreement of the first kind.

Premise P (physical unity). A system's contents are unified only if, for every two regions whose contents overlap and in every window of the contents' own time scale, some content-bearing carrier of each region responds gradedly, above noise, to a carrier of the other, and the coupling between them shrinks their disagreement within that window. Different carriers and moments may serve the two directions and different overlaps.

In short, the regions that contribute to one experience must be held together by a physical coupling that feels small changes above noise and pulls disagreements back, and not by an exchange of symbols. P is proposed as a necessary condition for unity. It concerns how conscious contents are held together; which contents are conscious, and what they are like, lie outside it. It says nothing about where in the brain unified contents live: it constrains whichever regions carry them, whether they span the cortex or are confined to a posterior zone of it (Koch et al., 2016).

A finer grain of function. P is still a functional condition: it picks out unity by what physical parts do to one another. What sets it apart is the level of detail, or grain, at which it describes them. Functionalism leaves the grain open. Described coarsely enough, a nation whose citizens exchange messages by radio could run a brain's program (Block, 1978), while the biology of cognition has been argued to tie mental states to a finer grain (Godfrey-Smith, 2016). Grain includes time: a radio nation standing in for a brain would run the right program at the wrong pace, still settling where the bird was after it had flown, and P's content window excludes it on that ground alone. P sits at the grain of graded physical dynamics, and computational functionalism about unity at the grain of the algorithm. Arguments that consciousness depends on embodiment, biology or the substrate often leave open which physical property does the work. P names one and states it as a mechanism: what a system's own readers take in, through what margin, against what noise and within what window. The closest precedent argues that, if physical dynamics matters to consciousness, processors designed to suppress deviations from their computational dynamics cannot be conscious (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2024). P supplies the scale at which suppression counts, the parts' own noise, adds that the coupling must restore agreement, and puts both to a test in cortex. A substrate requirement then becomes something to measure, by one protocol in cortex and in chips, and to test against a specified rival model. For cortex the two grains agree. They come apart for a digital simulation of cortex: it can reproduce the course in which the contents agree, while every bit inside it stays well clear of its threshold, so that small physical changes to one bit reach no other. The experiment of Section 6 asks which grain unity tracks. It reconnects two brain regions through a graded or a digital link, varies bandwidth and quantization separately, and tests an explicit model in which only bandwidth, delay and nonlinearity matter.

The argument. The case for P has three parts, defended in Section 3.

• Wholeness, an account of unity: unified experiences are parts of one total experience. A physical account should therefore say what physically makes them belong together.

• Counting, our hypothesis about what does: regions belong to one physical whole when chains of mutual responses above noise join the carriers of their contents. For a direct link, every change of a carrier between its noise and its threshold must reach the other.

at every instant would count no network of spiking cells as one system. P asks instead that some carrier of each region register the other regions within each window of the content's time scale.

The paper makes three claims: 1.

P predicts that a bridge which restores unified experience between two cortical regions supplies graded coupling and restores agreement within the content's window; a bridge certified to lack that coupling which still preserves a calibrated readout of unity challenges P and its readout assumption together. A specified dynamical model tests whether bandwidth, delay and quantization explain the readout instead (Section 6). 2. Under a noisy margin, a small physical change moves the next content's distribution by at most the probability of coming near a threshold, a bound that is attained. Digital readouts held within their margins fail the response test, while membrane models, including fits to recordings from awake mice, reach sensitive states within a percept's time scale (Section 3). 3. Enforced agreement must arrive before the content changes, so P predicts that cortical coupling relaxes within 166 ms across the cortex; on a noisy sheet of coupled oscillators, the coupling's reach decides how far agreement in phase holds (Section 4).

The formal results listed in Appendix K are machine-checked in Lean 4. The link to experience is carried by the realization hypothesis and the readout assumption, and the tests are designed to put both at risk.

2 Unity as agreement between overlapping regions

Think of an atlas. Each page maps one patch of ground, neighbouring pages overlap, and where they overlap they show the same roads. Pages that agree on every overlap fit together into one map of the whole territory. We treat the brain's regions the same way. Each describes part of a shared situation, and we propose that unity, on the side of content, is this agreement: local descriptions that match wherever they overlap. When they match, they fix a single description of the whole.

Synchrony is not unity: two regions can oscillate in phase while encoding a stimulus at two different locations. Unity is about what overlapping regions describe, and synchrony is at most one route to it.

Carriers and traces. A region's content is a variable the system itself reads, not merely one an outside observer can decode: the regions it drives respond to it, and it determines the quantity the region represents, such as a location. A variable that meets both conditions is a carrier; one that only an observer can decode is a trace. The supply current of a digital circuit reveals enough about its logical state to recover a secret key (Kocher et al., 1999), yet no gate reads it, so it is a trace. In cortex, membrane potentials and spike times are carriers, because the cells they drive integrate them. The same test says when a variable is a carrier: at the moments its readers take it in. Feed-forward inhibition confines a pyramidal cell's integration of its inputs to a window of a few milliseconds (Pouille & Scanziani, 2001; Gabernet et al., 2005), short against the interval between the spikes it receives (König et al., 1996), and the timing of first spikes in somatosensory cortex carries information about a stimulus that the spike count does not (Panzeri et al., 2001). A clocked latch, by contrast, looks at its input only during a short aperture at the clock edge. The input's value there is a carrier. The course of the voltage between edges, which nothing reads, is a trace, like the supply current. So a carrier's next content is what its readers take from it next, at the time they take it: for a membrane, the time of its next spike; for a node that feeds a latch, its value at the next clock edge.

Agreement is measured between regions whose contents represent a shared variable. The regions, and each one's content variable, are fixed by this causal role and by decodability before any agreement is measured. Nobody can make the measurement trivial by choosing the regions after the fact.

A running example. A visual area represents the bird's location on a retinotopic map, and a parietal area represents the same location to plan a reach. Each area's content is its estimate of the location, carried by the membrane potentials and spike times of the cells that encode it. Compatible content, here, is the two estimates agreeing.

The definition, stated precisely. Region i carries a content s i , a description of the variables it represents, and regions i and j overlap in the variables both represent. Restricting a content to an overlap keeps only the shared variables. The contents are compatible when every two agree on their overlap, s i | i∩j = s j | i∩j . Compatible contents extend to exactly one global description whose restriction to each region is that region's content. Compatibility is our proposed correlate of unity, and the overlap discrepancy measures how far contents fall short of it: the largest distance between two contents restricted to a common overlap.

Approximate agreement still fixes one description: if every overlap discrepancy of real-valued contents is at most ε, a weighted average of the contents that cover each variable is within ε of every region's content. Agreement is measured by decoding, and two accurate decoders agree whatever produced their agreement, since |d A -d B | ≤ |e A |+|e B | for errors e A and e B . The measure is therefore the agreement in excess of what the two errors imply. These results are proved in a companion paper (Bobadilla-Suarez, 2026), and P adds a condition on how that agreement is produced.

Two stages. The companion paper tests whether excess decoded agreement tracks unified content.

The bridge of Section 6 then tests how that agreement is physically produced. Moving from either to experience needs a readout checked against reports of unity while visibility, attention and task performance are varied (Section 6). If decoded agreement fails the companion's test, the experiential test falls back on that report readout. In animals, behaviour tests integration across regions and the mechanism behind it.

3 Enforced agreement and computed agreement

The argument in outline. Five definitions make "physically enforced" precise. Two theorems then show that content read from bits barely responds to small changes, first without noise and then with it. Next comes the case for the premise: wholeness asks for a physical realization, counting says what that realization is, and restoration adds a deadline. Finally, one measurement protocol, applied to a cortical membrane and to a logic node, shows where each substrate's carriers pass.

Definitions. Each is stated in words first.

• Micro state and content. A system has a physical state, its micro state x = (x i ) i , made up of the states x i of its regions. One step of its physics carries x to f (x). A content map π reads each region's content off the micro state. The content level is closed when the next content can be computed from the current content alone, without looking at the micro state: π • f = g • π for some content dynamics g. A digital computer's logical level is closed by design. The next content π(f (x)) of a carrier is what its readers take from it next.

• Noise margin. A readout has a noise margin on a set of states when each state in it has a neighbourhood on which the readout is constant, as any voltage well above a bit's threshold reads as 1.

• Graded dependence. Content depends gradedly on a region when arbitrarily small changes to that region can move the next content. Formally, no neighbourhood of the region's micro state leaves the next content unchanged while the other regions are held fixed.

• Contraction. The overlap discrepancy contracts near a state when one step of f shrinks it by a factor below one throughout a neighbourhood of that state, so perturbations too small to cross any threshold are pulled back toward agreement along with larger ones.

• Physical enforcement. Agreement is physically enforced at a state when content depends gradedly on each overlapping region there and the overlap discrepancy contracts nearby. These are two separate requirements: feeling small changes, and pulling disagreement back. P applies them carrier by carrier and window by window: in each content window some carrier reaches across each overlap in each direction, and the coupling restores agreement within the window.

The margin lemma. In words: content read through a margin cannot feel small enough physical changes. Precisely, if the micro dynamics is continuous and carries a state into a margin's operating set, the next content depends gradedly on no region's micro state. The proof takes one line: continuity carries a small enough neighbourhood of each region's micro state into the neighbourhood on which the readout is constant. A finite word of thresholded quantities has a margin away from its thresholds, so the lemma covers contents read from bits away from their thresholds. The lemma is mathematics; why it should matter for unity is argued below.

Noise. A noisy threshold's chance of flipping can vary smoothly with its input voltage even inside a nominal margin. Its next-content probability can therefore retain a small physical dependence that the exact margin lemma discards. P is read on response probabilities relative to the source's noise.

The response of a content to a region at scale η is the largest change that moving the region by at most η makes to the probability of any outcome of the next content, a total-variation distance. The yardstick for a large response is the response that a shift of one standard deviation produces in a Gaussian carrier, 2Φ(1/2) -1 = 0.38, and call it the fluctuation: a response this large moves the content by as much as the content naturally fluctuates. Graded dependence above the noise floor asks the response to reach the fluctuation for every change of the region that is larger than its own noise and smaller than the change that crosses one of its thresholds. When the region moves a carrier linearly under additive noise whose density has a single peak, Gaussian or heavy-tailed, a larger change moves the content at least as much as a smaller one, and the criterion is met exactly when a change of one noise amplitude reaches the fluctuation (Appendix C treats noise whose law changes with the state). No constant is fitted to either substrate.

The noisy margin theorem. The margin lemma has a noisy form, and it is this form that carries the argument. Let each realization of the noise fix an L-Lipschitz step of the micro dynamics, one that stretches no distance by more than a factor L. Let the content be constant within radius r of the noisy successor, except on a set of realizations of probability at most ε. Then a change of one region smaller than r/L moves the probability of every outcome of the next content by at most ε. For anything computed from bits, ε is the probability that some bit of the noisy successor lands within δ of its threshold, and the bound is attained. We call ε the margin exception probability. It counts every near approach to a threshold, including those that still produce the right bit, so it can exceed the chip's error rate and has to be checked on its own. A readout fails the response criterion when two things hold: ε is below the fluctuation, and some change larger than the source's noise still fits inside r/L. That change is then a witness, big enough to count and too small to matter.

The simulation objection.

A digital consensus algorithm can pull disagreement between contents back, and a simulation can follow a field's course more precisely than biological noise over any window we observe. The course of the contents alone therefore leaves the two unseparated. P looks one level down, at the physical carriers of those contents: the bits inside a simulation, held within their margins, fail the response test even while the simulated contents agree. Which carriers are tested, and how, is therefore part of the argument. Nudging a graded input to the simulation and nudging the voltage of one of its internal bits are different tests, as the replacement analysis below shows.

Wholeness and its realization. On the wholeness view, experiences are unified when they are parts of a single total experience (Bayne, 2010). Their belonging together is a relation among the contents, not one more item represented alongside them. A physical account of that relation has to say which carriers take part, how they act on one another, and over what time they form a whole. Counting answers that the carriers are sensitive to one another. The motivation is the springs of the introduction. When several regions describe the same graded variable, a coupling can hold their descriptions together through every variation physics can tell apart: move one, and the others respond, while a restoring pull keeps the shared variable consistent.

Why this criterion and not another. Each part of P can be seen at work by adding the parts one at a time and asking what each rules out. Plain causal dependence lets in almost everything: a one-way relay, a common broadcast, a clerk who reconciles the books once a day, and a digital circuit, since changing an input bit changes what its readers compute. Asking that the dependence run both ways and arrive within the content's own window rules out the relay, the broadcast and the slow clerk: an influence that runs one way, or lands after the content has changed, enforces nothing about that content. The window is set by how long the content lasts, so it bites hardest when the world sets the pace. A nation of citizens relaying a brain's signals by radio (Block, 1978) could run the right program, but put in a brain's place, with a human reaction time at every relay, it would still be computing where the bird was long after the bird had gone. Asking the coupling to contract disagreement rules out circuits that amplify it. What survives is fast, reciprocal, restoring dependence, and a digital consensus algorithm on a chip has all three, since its logic settles in nanoseconds. Only the last requirement, sensitivity across the whole range between noise and threshold, separates it from cortex. The margin condition therefore does one job, and its hardest test is a fast, accurate digital replacement (Appendix E).

Counting: one whole, measured at the noise floor. Two carriers are directly coupled when every admissible change of either, larger than its own noise and smaller than its threshold, moves the other's next content by at least the fluctuation. Changes are applied to the coordinates that carry content, in both directions where both are possible, and a carrier must admit at least one such change for the test to apply. A constitutive component is a set of carriers joined by chains of direct couplings.

Three things recommend this criterion. First, it intervenes on a variable the system itself reads, so the verdict belongs to the system and survives a change of the observer's decoder. Second, the noise and the threshold mark out the range over which a carrier can vary without changing category, and we propose that graded contents hold one another in place when each responds to the other across that whole range. Third, chains let an intermediate graded reader join two regions, and the window ties the relation to how long a content lasts. The criterion's strength is that one intervention protocol applies to every substrate. Its commitment about experience is that unity requires this kind of constraint even when a coarser causal organization produces the same reports.

Records in the coupling graph.

A record is a content held by a margin. Records still take part in ordinary cause and effect, through changes of their symbols. Under the noisy-margin hypotheses above, counting treats them in three ways.

• A region whose content is held by a margin, with an exception probability below the fluctuation, is coupled to no region that admits a change above its noise inside the margin, whatever the regions it reads carry. It shares a component only with itself.

• For any set of such records, two regions share a component exactly when a chain of couplings avoiding every record joins them. A rule that reads records and writes records adds more isolated vertices, not links.

• When a region's next content depends on another only through such a record's symbol, a change inside the margin moves it by at most the record's exception probability. Writing a correction back through that symbol keeps the same bound.

Graded readers join.

A region whose content moves with two regions above their noise, and moves them in turn, joins their components even when they share no direct coupling. Under linear dynamics with uniform noise such a reader joins two regions that a record reading the same two leaves apart (Appendix K). A register holding the bird's location as a number is a record; a cell that integrates spike times from the visual and parietal areas and projects back to both is a candidate graded reader. It joins them when the measured responses meet the criterion in each direction. A workspace built from reliable records can still make contents jointly accessible; on P, whether they form one physical whole is settled by the coupling graph and the restoring dynamics.

A precedent: clusters in a gas. Physics already counts systems by comparing an interaction with the parts' own fluctuations. In the theory of imperfect gases, two molecules belong to one physical cluster when their attraction outweighs the kinetic energy of their relative thermal motion, and a cluster is a set of molecules joined by chains of such bonds (Hill, 1955; Sator, 2003). Molecules whose attraction is weaker than their thermal motion still interact, and that interaction changes the pressure of the gas, yet it joins them into no cluster. The precedent is the method: compare a coupling with the parts' own fluctuations, and join parts through chains. The gas criterion counts bound clusters of molecules; counting applies the same method to carriers of content, and its bearing on experience rests on the argument above.

From coupling to P. When overlap is symmetric, graded dependence across every overlap in both directions is equivalent to direct mutual coupling across every overlap. Membership in one component then follows through chains, though a chain can join two regions that have no direct link. For regions with many carriers, the condition asks only that some carrier reach each overlapping region, in each direction, within every content window. The two directions may use different carriers and moments, which is weaker than asking every carrier to pass, as a formal example shows. P then adds that the coupling must shrink disagreement in time. The connectivity result covers the sensitivity half, and restoration is tested separately.

The chip, counted. A logic node of 1 fF at room temperature has thermal noise of 2 mV (Johnson, 1928; Nyquist, 1928), and the textbook inverter's margin is 506 times that. A change of one noise amplitude flips the bit with probability below 10 -100 (Kish, 2002). With margins maintained at the readouts, the response test isolates each bit in the constitutive graph. The bits still act on one another through their logical updates, which run on the chip's interacting voltages; what they lack is a response to small changes in one another (Appendix D).

Where the line falls. The same test is applied inside each substrate. A membrane's spike time can respond gradedly near threshold, while a count read through a maintained margin is a record. The membrane calculations below find how often a membrane is in a sensitive state, and an analog crossbar's column currents are another candidate carrier. Whether any of these contributes to P also depends on what downstream cells or arrays read, and on whether the shared content is restored (Section 5).

The membrane, counted. A spike time passes the test at the moment the membrane rises through threshold, where one unitary cortical input shifts the spike by 1.5 times its jitter (Appendix C). To see how often a membrane is in such a state, the protocol applied to the logic node is applied to a leaky integrate-and-fire membrane driven by white noise, over every state it occupies, with time constants of 5 to 20 ms (Destexhe & Paré, 1999; Destexhe et al., 2003) and rates of 0.5 to 8 Hz (Hromádka et al., 2008). It sits on average 2.0 to 3.5 noise amplitudes below threshold and passes at 0.013 to 2.4% of the states it occupies (Appendix F). A bit restored to a rail passes at none. No single bit can pass when the noise of the step that reads it includes one amplitude of the change: asked in both directions, its response under Gaussian noise is at most Φ(1) -1/2 = 0.34, the binary ceiling, below the fluctuation.

Rarely at an instant, often within a window. A stationary membrane enters a passing state within 400 ms, the integration time that precedes a conscious percept, with probability 0.085 to 0.997, even when the region it depends on supplies only 1/16 of its noise variance. At least one of 10 independent carriers then reaches the target region within such a window with probability at least 0.59, while at a single instant even 1000 carriers does so with probability as low as 0.025. That is why P is stated per window. The independent-carrier sweep also covers shorter windows. The 20 ms threshold for perceiving the order of two events (Hirsh & Sherrick, 1961) supplies a comparison scale: at least one of 1000 independent carriers reaches the other region more often than not from a window of 3 ms upward, and at 20 ms with probability at least 0.98.

Recorded membranes. Whole-cell recordings from 86 excitatory cells of the barrel cortex of awake mice in quiet wakefulness (Kiritani et al., 2023) constrain a membrane model's noise, time constant and slow drive. Applying the response protocol to that fitted model tests the declared ranges (Appendix F). The median cell sits 3.7 noise amplitudes below its threshold, farther than the declared 2.0 to 3.5, and its fitted model passes at 0.15% of sampled states, inside the declared range. That model predicts 0.47 times the median cell's recorded firing rate: recorded membranes fire more readily than the Gaussian model from which their passing states are read. At a noise share of 1/16 it enters a passing state within 400 ms with probability 0.15, and at least one of 10 independent model carriers drawn from these cells reaches the target within that window with probability at least 0.91.

Readers, shared input and switching nodes. Three variations leave the verdict where it is (Appendix F). A reader that registers only whether the membrane fired within the window finds it passing at 0.013 to 2.4% of its states; if every cortical reader pooled spikes only over windows longer than a content's time scale, P would deny unity to cortex, and that would count against P. With shared input up to 0.75 of the noise variance, above the correlation of neighbouring membranes in quiet wakefulness (Poulet & Petersen, 2008), at least one of 1000 model carriers supplies a directed reach within 400 ms with probability at least 0.98. And a chip's nodes, which pass through their thresholds many times in every window, pass at the voltage as a membrane does, since a change of one noise amplitude moves a crossing by one jitter. The voltage is not what the chip reads, though. Timing closure keeps every transition outside the setup-and-hold window of the latch that reads the node (Ginosar, 2011), so the latch reads the restored bit, which passes at no state and in no window. The separation holds at every yardstick from 0.01 to 0.6 (Figure 2). What separates the membrane from the restored bit is the distance from threshold at which each is held when it is read: a few noise amplitudes, against 506.

Categories. Categorical contents, such as the dominant percept in binocular rivalry, have margins in every substrate, so P is stated on the graded variables from which categories are read, such as the relative strength of competing percepts. A graded variable stored in a reliable word of bits is read through margins again.

Gradual replacement.

Replacing neurons one by one with units that behave exactly as they do tests any substrate condition (Chalmers, 1995). The hardest case is a recurrent controller whose resolution is finer than biological noise, with enough bandwidth and the natural delay. Its output can respond gradedly, above noise, to a cortical input, even while every bit inside it keeps a wide voltage margin. P therefore looks at the carriers of content and their readers at each interface, and its digital exclusion applies only where margins are maintained there. Appendix E works this through, including what preserved reports would mean.

What the premise rests on. The case for P is that unified graded contents must hold one another in place, physically, across their whole range of variation, and be pulled back into agreement before they change. The formal results turn that into a precise consequence for readouts held within margins. The membrane computations, including fits to recorded potentials, show that cortex has candidate sensitive states. The bridge tests the proposal together with a calibrated readout of unity, against a model that explains integration by bandwidth, delay and nonlinear transmission (Section 6).

Other accounts of unity, such as joint access (Bayne, 2010), make their own predictions once each is given an implementation and a readout model.

4 When and how far a coupling enforces agreement P asks two things of the coupling: it must pull the disagreement of unified contents back before the content changes, and it must reach every pair of regions whose contents are unified. The first gives the prediction that the restoration test of Section 6 checks; the second says over what distances that test should find restoration.

Agreement in time.

A correction that arrives after the content has changed enforces agreement on a content already replaced, so enforced agreement has a deadline. Two things limit how soon it arrives. It arrives no sooner than the coupling's causal cone allows: a site can track a variable at another only after enough rounds of the coupling to place the second site in its causal past. And it arrives at the coupling's relaxation rate: a coupling that shrinks the overlap discrepancy by a factor κ < 1 per step brings a discrepancy of d 0 within ε after log(d 0 /ε)/ log(1/κ) steps, and one that shrinks it by no more than ρ per step needs at least log(d 0 /ε)/ log(1/ρ). In cortex, signal travel typically takes 18 to 31 ms of the 400 ms that precede a conscious percept, so the deadline falls on the relaxation time (Appendix B). P therefore predicts a cortical relaxation time of at most 160 to 166 ms across the cortex, as signals take the slower or the faster fibres, and 171 ms within a posterior zone. A restoration slower than these counts against P.

Reach. The regions to be joined lie up to 15 cm apart if a scene's contents span the cortex, and about 5 cm apart if they are confined to a posterior zone. On a sheet of coupled oscillators sharing one natural frequency, in the harmonic approximation, the variance of the phase difference between two sites is the noise strength times their effective resistance, the resistance a meter would read if each coupling were a wire of the coupling's conductance. Under coupling of bounded range the resistance grows at least logarithmically with distance, the Gaussian form of the absence of true long-range order in two dimensions (Mermin & Wagner, 1966), while a kernel whose tail falls off more slowly than r -4 bounds it at every distance (Chung & Fuchs, 1951; Kunz & Pfister, 1976). A Lipschitz encoder carries phase agreement to content agreement: at noise strength D the root-meansquare content discrepancy is at most L √ D R eff (Appendix A). In cortex the long-range coupling is synaptic, since the field of a local source falls below detection within millimetres (Appendix I).

Local unity and switching. The regions whose contents are unified may form one patch of cortex, or several patches joined through a hub. Counting then looks at the carriers entering and leaving the hub. A hub that passes only records drops out of the graph and leaves the patches disconnected, one way to realize the switch model of the split brain (Bayne, 2010). A hub whose complete inputoutput response passes the graded test can join the patches, even if it attends to them in turn, provided its readers' timing and memory still let disagreement be pulled back within a content window.

The thalamus is the natural candidate hub. Its relay cells fire in two modes (Sherman, 2001). In the tonic mode the output follows the input nearly linearly (Lesica & Stanley, 2004). In the burst mode the cell answers with an all-or-none burst, typically when excitation follows a prolonged inhibition (Lesica & Stanley, 2004), and it can burst again only after a renewed hyperpolarization (Sherman, 2001). The protocol of Section 3, applied to a model relay cell with both modes (Smith et al., 2000) at matched rates, orders them: within 400 ms a tonic cell enters a passing state at least 2.3 times as often as a bursting one, in every declared regime (Appendix F). Tonic mode therefore offers more chances for a passing route, a prediction to test on relay cells recorded in each mode. P predicts an effect on unity only where that difference decides whether the whole route meets the window and restoration requirements. The same protocol applies to a router between analog patches, whose representation and timing decide which graded changes reach its downstream readers. A bridge across a putative hub tests that whole route.

5 Current artificial systems

A clocked digital chip stores records protected by noise margins and updates them through causal connections between gates. When its readouts stay within the noisy-margin hypotheses, small voltage changes produce responses below the yardstick. A transformer running on such hardware inherits this for its internal logical contents, even when its algorithm pulls disagreements together. A chip tracking the bird holds each area's estimate as a word of bits, and the two words agree when a step of the program copies or averages one into the other; between steps, neither moves with the voltages beneath the other. Hardware whose contents are graded physical quantities coupled without barriers, such as analog, in-memory or neuromorphic substrates, can satisfy P. Satisfying it means that such a substrate's contents, the column currents of an analog crossbar for instance, are held together physically; it does not determine whether any of them is experienced, or whether any is like a human percept.

Symbols and physical contents. The line P draws is between symbolic and physical content, and the line between digital and analog hardware is its most common instance. A symbol, in the sense the margin lemma makes precise, is a content read through a noise margin: a physical state whose identity survives every small enough change of the state that carries it, so two symbols agree only when a rule makes them agree. A physical content is a graded quantity that the system's own dynamics reads, so its agreement with the contents it overlaps is produced by the coupling between them. A bit and a spike count latched at a clock edge are symbols; a spike time, a membrane potential and the phase of a coupled oscillator are physical contents.

Organisation, not material. The criterion concerns how a substrate is organised, not what it is made of. An analog crossbar whose column currents settle through shared conductances, or an array of coupled electronic or optical oscillators, couples its contents as a cortical sheet does. A neuromorphic chip passes if its coupled membrane potentials do. A latched count is judged at its reader, with that reader's noise, margin and integration window, and a neural circuit whose readouts kept the same margins would be excluded in the same way. In analog in-memory accelerators, a layer's products are currents summed on the lines of a memory array and then digitized: in a 64core phase-change chip each row's current is converted into integers, and the traffic between cores runs on those integers (Le Gallo et al., 2023). The words passed between cores are tested at their logical readouts; whether the channel as a whole couples the analog variables of two arrays is tested at those arrays' readers, as for the cortical bridge.

Why spikes are not bits. What makes all-or-none spikes graded carriers is their timing. When a membrane rises through threshold, the moment it crosses moves continuously with any small input, and receiving cells integrate spike times as they arrive. A clock alone does not separate the substrates: a spike time read through a clock still passes near threshold. What a digital circuit adds is restoration. Each gate drives its output back to a rail, so every transition a latch reads starts and ends far from any threshold. Clockless logic fails in the same way: its transition times move with every voltage, but its values are read from completed codes held at rails (Appendix G).

Leakage and the margin's width. Supply noise, crosstalk and temperature do move the voltages beneath digital readouts. While the theorem's hypotheses hold, their effect on the next logical content is capped by the margin exception probability. Each gate pulls its output back to a rail, and the logic network coordinates values across rails; this makes no bit respond to small changes in another. The width of the margin decides which physical disturbances the bound covers, and the precision of a represented number is a separate matter from the voltage margin of each bit (Appendix G).

Attractor basins. Cortex has margins of its own. An attractor network's basin is a dynamical margin: which attractor the network settles in survives every small enough change. The basin gives the attractor's label a margin, but it leaves graded the state that carries the label: the position along a continuous attractor, such as a bump of activity that encodes a direction, and the membrane potentials and spike times within the basin, which downstream cells integrate. A cortical circuit whose contents were read only as attractor labels, far from the basins' boundaries, would fall under the margin lemma as a chip does, and the weak nudge of Section 6 tests which case cortex is in.

6 Tests The readout assumption. A bridge changes a physical mechanism, and inferring anything about experience from it also needs a model of observation. Assumption R: within the tested interventions, a subject's calibrated reports of one simultaneous field spanning the two regions remain evidence about experienced unity. Calibration separates those reports from reports of local visibility, the ability to report from each region, attention, and success on each component task. The criterion is fixed in advance and applied equally to natural coupling, artificial bridges and gradual replacement. Appendix H specifies the time-resolved report calibration and the competing switching account used to assess this readout. Under R, if a bridge certified to remove P's coupling leaves reports of unity intact, P and R are challenged together, and the experiment commits to reading that outcome as a challenge. The same reading applies to gradual replacement. In animals, matching across two fields measures the integration of information and tests the mechanism; a human preparation adds reports of unity. Once the companion has validated it, decoded agreement serves as a neural correlate, with its decoder held fixed across interventions. The limits of R are stated in Section 8.

Separating coupling from information.

In every manipulation of cortex available so far, graded coupling and information move together, and stimulating the regions from outside does not separate them. Coherence between cortical regions arises largely from communication between them (Schneider et al., 2021), and where in-phase transcranial stimulation of two regions raised their synchrony, it raised directed information flow with it (Reinhart & Nguyen, 2019). The coupling has to be supplied instead.

The bridge.

Interrupt the natural connection between two regions, and reconnect them by stimulating each in proportion to the activity recorded at the other (Figure 1). The reconnection runs through one of two loops.

• The analog loop is an analog filter and amplifier driving the stimulator, analog end to end, so its output moves with every graded change in its input.

• The quantized loop is the same filter and amplifier with a quantizer between them, so its output is read from bits and has a margin.

Both loops share the output stage and stimulation path. The design is factorial: each bandwidth is run with and without the quantizer. Within that family one pair is chosen to control information, as described next, and further blocks sweep the quantizer's step at fixed bandwidth and delay.

Matching the information.

In the information-controlled pair, the analog loop carries no more estimated transfer entropy or task information than the quantized loop; its bandwidth is lowered to achieve this while it still settles within the content window, and with held stimuli it also adds noise of its own, below the level at which it would fail P (Appendix H). Whether each loop passes P is a separate question, answered on the full circuit: each direction is tested at the actual downstream reader, including that reader's memory and integration time. Transfer entropy counts everything one region's activity tells about the other's, and the loops could match it and still differ in how much of the task gets through. So the task variable is also decoded from the activity each loop evokes in the region it drives, and the loops count as matched when the analog loop carries no more information than the quantized one, in total or about the task. Both loops were simulated on a model pair of regions, with a linear and a nearest-neighbour estimator of each quantity. At a step of 10 noise amplitudes, a cutoff between 17 and 95 Hz matches the linear estimate of transfer entropy in every simulated regime whose task variable spans at least half a step. At that cutoff the analog loop carries less task information than the quantized one by either estimator, and less transfer entropy by the nearest-neighbour one. Matching these two summaries is a control and leaves the outcome open: the dynamical alternative below works from the full delivered signal and can still predict different outcomes for matched loops.

A competing mechanism. The alternative is a recurrent observer. Each region's estimate combines its own local evidence with the signal the bridge delivers, updated with a finite delay, a fitted gain and noise, and a decision rule reads the difference between the estimates (Appendix H). The filter and quantizer enter only through their measured effect on the signal. The observer's parameters are fitted on pilot blocks and then frozen, and it is scored on held-out bandwidths, quantizer resolutions and perturbations, predicting both choices and recovery from disagreement. It can favour either arm through timing and nonlinearity alone, and gives no special role to sensitivity inside a margin.

Certifying the contrast. P asks for a carrier response somewhere within each content window, so each loop is classified by the probability of visiting a passing state in each direction, together with the measured restoration of disagreement. A loop can spend little time in passing states and still visit them often. Every candidate route counts: threshold crossings, joint words, repeated samples and residual biological paths. To exclude a loop, the response bound must cover the complete map to the next readout, memory included; to include one, the measured carriers must also restore agreement (Appendix H). Both arms use the same noise scale, interventions and content window.

A task variable that varies continuously crosses the quantizer's edges and visits a passing state in almost every window, so the task holds each stimulus at the centre of a quantizer step for the trial, and the quantized loop's own record of its input sorts its trials into those that visited a passing state and those that did not.

Predictions and outcomes. Take blocks in which the analog bridge restores the calibrated unity readout. P with R predicts that a quantized bridge certified to lack the required coupling will lose that readout. The recurrent observer predicts the readout from the transmitted signals through its frozen decision rule. The decisive blocks are those in which the two predictions diverge while local visibility and report ability stay intact. Preserved unity reports there challenge P with R. An analog advantage there favours P only if the observer fails to account for it within its preregistered uncertainty. If both bridges pass the coupling test, equal performance is what P expects. If the analog bridge fails to restore integration, the positive control has failed and the comparison is uninformative.

In animals, accuracy constrains the observer's predictions and the perturbation measurements test P's physical conditions; the experiential comparison rests on R's calibration in humans. A stable stimulation code can also be learned as a symbol; a readout restored that way improves over sessions and is lost when the quantizer's levels are relabelled, whereas one restored by coupling is present from the first bridged blocks and follows the relabelling (Appendix H).

A first preparation. Closed loops that trigger stimulation at one cortical site from spikes recorded at another already run for days in behaving animals (Jackson et al., 2006; Guggenmos et al., 2013); the analog arm replaces the trigger with a continuous drive. A first preparation places chronic arrays in two areas that represent a shared variable, such as the visual and parietal areas that represent the bird's location, interrupts the natural connection between them at its terminals (Appendix H), and alternates bandwidth and quantization conditions across blocks in the same animal. Directed perturbations check for residual routes before the interruption is treated as a disconnection. Transfer entropy (Schreiber, 2000) is estimated from each block's recordings, and the step, the cutoff and the The displayed pair uses the quantizer's step, the analog cutoff and noise added in the analog arm to control estimated transfer entropy and task information; the full comparison also tests both arms at common bandwidths. What leaks from the stimulator into a recording contact is removed by subtracting the loop's own output, passed through the measured transfer. The loop from B to A is the same. analog loop's noise are set on pilot blocks. The primary animal readout is behavioural integration: a task requiring the values the two areas represent to be combined, such as judging whether stimuli in their two fields match. Blocks with the connection interrupted and neither loop running come first, as a positive control: the comparison is informative only if the analog loop restores some of the integration that interruption removes. The companion's excess decoded agreement is the neural readout. At the declared effect sizes the behavioural comparison is the weaker, needing 1248 trials per loop for a pairwise comparison; the factorial design and the equivalence margins for preserved reports need a power calculation on pilot data. The loops record and stimulate in separate frequency bands, so the recordings stay readable under a continuous drive (Appendix H).

A weak nudge should spread. Nudge a content-bearing variable in one region, in either direction, by anything from the source's noise amplitude up to its threshold, and measure the next content read in an overlapping region. P predicts that within the content window some carrier responds by at least the declared yardstick, and that the shared variable moves back toward agreement. Transcranial alternating current and weak intracortical fields are candidate interventions. The decoded variable is graded, read by the region's own targets, and calibrated against the source's noise. A response that widens the disagreement challenges the restoring half of P; a valid upper bound below the yardstick throughout the window challenges its sensitivity half. The rival observer is tested on the same intervention time courses.

Agreement should be restored. Perturb one region and measure how fast its disagreement with its partners returns to the declared tolerance. P predicts restoration within the relaxation time of Section 4 for the admissible perturbations, with proportional restoring response in the linear regime. On an artificial system two kinds of perturbation are possible. Patching a represented activation changes a logical value and tests whether the algorithm restores agreement. Nudging an internal physical carrier within its margin tests the response bound. They act on different variables, as the replacement analysis shows.

The field's causal cone. The brain's electric field reaches the tissue with negligible propagation delay on neural time scales (Gratiy et al., 2017), while synaptic influence across the cortex takes at least 8 ms. Re-agreement faster than the synaptic route allows would reveal a non-synaptic part of the coupling. The field of a local source falls below detection within millimetres, so the cone is tested at millimetre distances, and at centimetres P predicts re-agreement through synaptic coupling, which is graded as well (Appendix I).

Split brain. Callosal section, read as divided perception with undivided consciousness (Pinto et al., 2017), contested (de Haan et al., 2020), or as consciousness alternating between the hemispheres (Bayne, 2010), removes graded coupling and information together, and the remaining subcortical routes carry both at once: the confound the bridge is built to break.

7 Related work

Appendix J relates P to accounts that tie consciousness to biology, to the analog-digital distinction and to field theories.

Indicator properties. Butlin et al. (2023) assess current AI systems against indicator properties of consciousness, each stated computationally, so every indicator sits at the grain of an algorithm. P adds one indicator stated at the grain of graded dynamics, a condition on how the substrate realises the others, so a system can have every computational indicator and fail P, as a faithful simulation of cortex does.

Levels of description.

Chandaria et al. ( 2026) distinguish an algorithm from the intrinsic causal structure of its physical implementation, and treat substrate requirements as constraints on which implementations can realise a functional role. P specifies a condition at that physical grain: contentbearing carriers must respond gradedly above their own noise and restore agreement within a content window. The relevant reciprocal influence therefore has a measured amplitude and time scale.

Computational closure. On the account of Rosas et al. (2024), a macroscopic level that is informationally, causally and computationally closed marks emergent software in a physical system. That closure is the property Section 3 finds at the content level of a digital system, and P reads it the other way round: a level closed off from the graded state beneath it is one whose agreement is computed, not enforced.

Designed to suppress its physics. Kleiner & Ludwig (2024) argue that if a system's physical dynamics is relevant to its consciousness, processors designed to suppress deviations from their computational dynamics cannot be conscious. The margin lemma states that suppression formally, and this paper adds a scale fixed by the parts' own noise, which counts systems instead of asking whether physics is relevant at all, a contraction condition, and a test in cortex.

Integrated information.

Integrated information theory also denies experience to digital simulations of a brain (Tononi & Koch, 2015; Findlay et al., 2024), through the causal structure of the hardware at the grain of its logic gates. P proposes sensitivity and restoration of graded contentbearing carriers as its constitutive condition, evaluated through the same response protocol on model membranes and logic nodes.

What physical tests can tell us. Love (2026) argues that third-person science cannot resolve why physical processes are experienced or settle the attribution of experience to another system, while its findings can inform practical judgments about that attribution. This paper works within that distinction: P is a proposed necessary condition for the unity of contents already taken to be conscious, and the bridge tests its physical mechanism together with an assumption about reports. Neither the response bounds nor their experimental tests solve the hard problem. A Russellianmonist reading, on which the intrinsic nature underlying physical dynamics matters to experience (Alter & Pereboom, 2023), is compatible with this use of measured dynamics to inform judgments about other systems; P does not identify that intrinsic nature.

8 Limitations

• The premise. P is a premise and is not derived from the dynamics; the cortical tests bear on whether it holds. It is necessary for unity and not sufficient for consciousness: coupled pendulums satisfy it. It constrains how a system's conscious contents are held together and is silent on which contents are conscious and what they are like. An analog crossbar that passes P holds its column currents together physically, which makes none of them an experience, still less one like a human percept.

• Wholeness and counting. Wholeness does not entail counting or contraction. Counting is a hypothesis about how unity is realized, stricter than ordinary causal dependence and stricter than failure to split into independent parts. The logical states of a digital network depend causally on one another, and a field may have a closed effective description. Our reasons for asking for sensitivity across the whole admissible range motivate P but do not prove that experience requires it. The gas analogy supports comparing coupling with fluctuations, not identifying physical clusters with subjects. Rejecting counting leaves the response bounds standing and removes their reading in terms of experience.

• Grain and functionalism. A functional account that includes the same response and restoration criterion agrees with P. Accounts built on temporal organization, nonlinear transmission or joint access can still reject its claim about what unity consists in. Matching two information summaries leaves those organizations different, so a successful alternative model remains a competitor, even when it tells the loops apart.

• Readouts and outcomes. R is an additional assumption linking calibrated reports to unity under the interventions tested. Behaviour can integrate information without the experience at issue here, so an animal matching task does not establish experiential unity, and a human report of unity needs visibility, attention and report ability controlled. A null result challenges P with R only when a bridge certified to lack the required coupling preserves the calibrated unity readout, with enough power to establish equivalence; giving up R would also give up the behavioural inference in gradual replacement. The proposed experiment cannot settle P independently of every readout assumption. Calibration against externally alternating stimuli constrains the report model but does not establish that those stimuli produce a particular experience, and switching faster than the calibrated temporal resolution can remain indistinguishable from simultaneous experience in both reports and recordings, which leaves the comparison inconclusive. An advantage for the analog arm is not enough evidence for P on its own, since bandwidth, delay and nonlinear transmission may explain it; the comparison needs predictions that diverge from the fitted alternative. If both bridges pass, equal outcomes are compatible with P. The positive control requires the analog loop to restore integration, stimulation can recruit cells synchronously or antidromically, and the recorded envelope samples only part of a region's carriers.

• Human evidence. The experiential comparison needs a human in whom the natural connection between two regions is interrupted and a bridge restores it. Intracranial recordings made for clinical monitoring leave that connection intact, and callosal section cannot be reversed, so the human arm awaits a clinical preparation that allows it, and the readout and the coupling classification still have to be validated in humans. The animal experiment tests P's physical conditions in the meantime. A hypothesis that ties unity to a particular tissue would be a different proposal from P's organizational criterion, and the electronic bridge leaves it untested.

• Hardware and contents. The digital exclusion needs the margin, Lipschitz and admissiblechange hypotheses to hold at the actual next readout, and at a cortical interface a highprecision converter can pass on perturbations above biological noise even though the processor's internal bits keep large margins (Appendix G). Which variables a system's own dynamics reads is settled system by system from its circuitry, and the margin lemma takes it as given; a cortex whose unified contents were attractor labels alone would fail P. Confirming the predictions for artificial systems checks that hardware runs inside its margins and leaves P untested; the tests of P are the cortical ones.

• Models. The cortical estimates model one integrate-and-fire membrane under white noise over declared ranges, and the recorded check covers one area of one species in one dataset (Appendix F). The bridge simulations use a one-directional transmission model with no spikes, stimulation artefact or plasticity, and leave the rival observer unfitted (Appendix H). Phase agreement over distance holds in the harmonic approximation, the relaxation time of cortical coupling is unmeasured, and the field's contribution across centimetres is a quantity to be measured (Appendices A, B and I). The scope of each model is stated with it.
