A Reach: resistance, encoders and simulations

The logarithmic growth is a lower bound for every kernel of bounded range. Group the sites into shells around a site a, so that the coupling joins only sites in the same or adjacent shells. The shells then act as conductors in series, and the effective conductance from a to any site beyond shell n is at most k<n 1/C k -1 , where C k is the coupling crossing from shell k to shell k + 1. On a planar sheet the perimeter of shell k grows linearly in k, so C k ≤ c (k + 1) for a constant c set by the kernel's strength and width, and the effective resistance is at least log(n + 1)/c. Widening the kernel enlarges its shells and raises c, which slows the growth and leaves it unbounded. Distanceindependent agreement on a sheet therefore needs coupling of unbounded range.

A tail slower than r -4 bounds the resistance at every distance. Run a chain of site sets out from a through discs of radius 2 j and back in to b, the two widest discs spanning the separation. The phase difference across a and b telescopes through the discs' mean phases, and the drop between the means of two consecutive discs is bounded by the coupling energy between them, shared among the pairs of their sites. A disc of radius 2 j on a planar sheet holds at least α 4 j sites, and a kernel K(r) ≳ r -(2+σ) couples two sites of consecutive discs by at least β 2 -(2+σ)j . The number of pairs grows as 16 j and their coupling falls as 2 -(2+σ)j , so the drops shrink geometrically with ratio q = 2 -(2-σ)/2 , which is below one for σ < 2, and the effective conductance is at least (1-q) 2 α 2 β/8 however far apart a and b lie.

Both results match classical potential theory. Imagine a random walker on the lattice that jumps between sites with probabilities proportional to the kernel, which is the same at every site. The resistance from a site to infinity is infinite exactly when that walker is sure to return to its start, that is, when the walk is recurrent (Doyle & Snell, 1984). Shorting every site outside a disc around a can only lower the resistance from a to a site b beyond the disc, so under recurrence that resistance grows without bound as b recedes. A symmetric kernel of finite second moment, which includes every tail steeper than r -4 , gives a recurrent walk in two dimensions (Chung & Fuchs, 1951). The bound above is the matching statement for tails slower than r -4 , whose walks escape. The same threshold holds beyond the harmonic approximation: the plane rotator in two dimensions with coupling falling as r -α , 2 < α < 4, has true long-range order at low noise (Kunz & Pfister, 1976), which short-range coupling forbids. With short-range coupling the plane-rotator sheet has a Kosterlitz-Thouless transition (Fröhlich & Spencer, 1981), an order-disorder crossover that the simulations below locate.

When natural frequencies differ from site to site, short-range coupling fares worse still: phases then desynchronize in every dimension up to four (Hong et al., 2005).

Two further properties bound the resistance from above. Adding coupling never raises it, and a direct coupling caps it at its reciprocal. Across a finite cortex a wide short-range kernel and a slow tail differ by a slowly growing logarithm, so telling them apart takes a measurement of the kernel's second moment as well as of its tail.

An encoder that reads the phases of a small neighbourhood relative to the phase at its centre does better than the Lipschitz bound of Section 4. It reports one content at every site of a travelling plane wave or a winding, whatever the gradient, and for a wave plus a departure from it its discrepancy between two sites is at most its Lipschitz constant times the departure's relative readings there, so it pays for the local roughness of the field and for nothing else. Both bounds read one oscillator population per content patch. Across centimetres, where two territories describing one quantity need not be neighbours on the sheet, that reading is an assumption, the phase-to-content assumption: each territory's content is read, by encoders of Lipschitz constant L that are equal where territories overlap, from the phase of one oscillator population assigned to it, so that the phase agreement of the two populations bounds the agreement of the two contents. It is a modelling choice about cortex, since the coupling of a field is spatial while two territories describing one quantity need not be neighbours. Under it the coupling's reach bounds phase disagreement between distant territories directly and content disagreement through it.

Simulated sheets at identical frequencies, of side 64 and 128, with nearest-neighbour, exponential and power-law kernels of tail exponent σ = 1 and σ = 3 at a common row sum, follow the harmonic identity in the ordered phase. The measured phase variance is at most 1.15 times D R eff at D = 0.1 and at most 1.26 times at D = 0.4, the excess rising with noise as the cosine coupling softens, and a logarithm fits its growth with distance better than a line in 16 of the 16 runs at those noise levels. At D = 1.2 the nearest-neighbour sheet disorders: the mean chord discrepancy ⟨1 -cos(θ a -θ b )⟩ at the largest separation is 1.00. The exponential and σ = 1 sheets stay ordered at that noise (0.46 and 0.50), and the σ = 3 sheet nearly disorders (0.92), so the kernel's width sets the order-disorder crossover as well as the rate of decay. Exact resistance sums at sheet sides 128, 512 and 1024 separate width from tail. The exponential kernel, with 25 times the nearest-neighbour stiffness, gives resistance at half the side of 0.531, 0.549 and 0.558, still growing; the σ = 1 tail gives 0.580, 0.577 and 0.577, and the σ = 3 tail, steeper than r -4 , gives 1.198, 1.448 and 1.572, growing as a short-range kernel does.

Scope. Phase variance equals effective resistance in the harmonic approximation at identical natural frequencies. The logarithmic lower bound is proved for kernels of bounded range, and the bound under a tail slower than r -4 for a sheet that supplies the site counts and couplings of a dyadic chain of discs. Unbounded resistance under a kernel of finite second moment is the classical recurrence criterion on the lattice; logarithmic growth is established numerically. Above the order-disorder crossover the harmonic identity fails. One oscillator population per content patch is a modelling choice about cortex.

B Agreement in time for cortex

The causal cone is stated precisely as follows: a report at one site that tracks a variable at another to within ε, for two values more than 2ε apart, is possible after T rounds of the coupling only if the second site lies in the first site's causal past for T rounds.

The longest cortico-cortical fibres run about 15 cm (Nunez & Srinivasan, 2014). Callosal axons conduct at median velocities of 4.9 to 8.8 m/s, and the fastest of them at up to 20 m/s (Caminiti et al., 2009). A chemical synapse adds about 0.5 ms (Katz & Miledi, 1965; Sabatini & Regehr, 1996). The earliest a synaptic signal can cross the cortex is therefore 8 ms, along the fastest axons, and typical arrival takes 18 to 31 ms. For the time scale of a content, take the unconscious integration that precedes a conscious percept, which lasts up to 400 ms (Herzog et al., 2016). Count agreement as reached when disagreement has fallen 10-fold, decaying exponentially. Agreement then arrives in time when the coupling's relaxation time is at most 160 ms with typical arrival along the slower fibres, and 166 ms along the faster. Over a localized extent of 5 cm the earliest arrival is 3 ms, typical arrival along the faster fibres is 6.2 ms, and the relaxation time may reach 171 ms. Signal travel thus uses only a small part of the time available, and whether agreement arrives in time depends on how fast the coupling settles.

Scope. The deadlines are proved for a given contraction factor, and identifying that factor with the coupling's spectral gap is linear response. The relaxation time of cortical coupling is unmeasured, and agreement is read as a declared reduction factor of disagreement.

C A single input and noise that changes with the state

A neuron in numbers. Suppose an input ∆V , too small to fire the cell on its own, arrives while the membrane potential is rising through threshold at rate V . It moves the spike by ∆V / V . Voltage noise σ V jitters the spike by σ V / V . The shift therefore exceeds the jitter exactly when ∆V exceeds σ V , whatever the slope, and spike generation adds little noise of its own (Mainen & Sejnowski, 1995). A unitary excitatory potential between cortical pyramidal cells averages 1.3 mV, with a coefficient of variation of 0.52 (Markram et al., 1997), and the membrane noise near threshold is 0.54 mV (Jacobson et al., 2005). Counting the input's own variability as noise, one such input shifts the spike by 1.5 times its jitter, a response of 0.55. Every input larger than 0.64 mV passes, up to the input that fires the cell.

Noise whose law changes with the state. When the law of the noise changes with the state, as the variance of a spike count does, a larger change still moves the content at least as much as a smaller one on each side of the state, provided the laws have a monotone likelihood ratio, as exponential families in their natural parameter do: such laws cross once along the parameter the region moves. The criterion of Section 3 is then met exactly when a change of one noise amplitude up and one down both reach the fluctuation.

D Counting in detail

The logic node. In the declared Gaussian model a change of one amplitude toward the threshold moves a restored bit by the fluctuation only at half an amplitude from the threshold, 0.099% of the margin's width. When both directions are admissible, their smaller response stays below the fluctuation at every distance, by the single-bit ceiling. The noisy margin theorem supplies the more general exclusion whenever the exception probability is below the yardstick and an admissible perturbation fits inside the effective margin. A readout that meets those hypotheses at every state in a window fails throughout the window.

The circuit still passes on changes of logical state, and crosstalk and supply noise still move its voltages. Counting isolates a reliable record only with respect to the stated physical interventions; both kinds of interaction remain in the full description of the chip. A reader that integrates several decisions is judged on its complete next-readout map, as in Appendix H.

Effective descriptions and causal dependence.

At the logical level a digital circuit has an update b ′ = g(b). The swap b ′1 = b 2 , b ′2 = b 1 couples its two bits causally: flip either input and the other output flips. Computational closure keeps this dependence and discards the voltage differences within a logical state. Closure, and ordinary failure to split into independent parts, therefore answer a different question from counting, which asks which physical changes that leave the content intact still reach another carrier above noise. A digital circuit's records are isolated in that sense while their logical values depend on one another.

A field can also have a closed effective description. Its case for P rests on how its selected carriers actually respond and restore. For every substrate, the content variables, their noise, the admissible interventions and the reader's integration time are fixed before the test. These choices give the count a physical meaning, and give a critic the quantities with which to challenge it.

E Gradual replacement

The strongest replacement is a recurrent digital controller that reproduces the relevant cortical dynamics to within biological noise, with enough bandwidth and the natural delay. Its converters resolve changes smaller than the noise on its cortical input, and its output drives the same downstream readers. Replacing neurons one by one with such units preserves functional organization at the grain used to predict behaviour (Chalmers, 1995).

Two interventions need to be kept apart. Changing the cortical input by one of its noise amplitudes can move many quantization levels and change the controller's output. Changing the voltage of an internal bit by one of its own noise amplitudes, inside its margin, leaves the next logical content almost unchanged. The margin theorem bounds the second under its hypotheses; more numerical precision makes the first finer without narrowing any internal bit's margin. P claims that the internal realization of content matters too. The motivation is mutual constraint among graded carriers (Section 3), and the demanding consequence is that an accurate logical emulation can reproduce the dynamics of content while lacking that internal relation. Applying this to a hybrid means first identifying which internal variables actually carry the relevant contents. Where the controller only relays signals between cortical carriers, those carriers' responses to one another are measured through the whole channel. A finely quantized channel may pass every admissible cortical change; being digital supplies no exclusion on its own. The resolution sweep therefore does two jobs. It tests the rival observer's prediction that performance improves as transmission error and delay shrink, and it finds where, if anywhere, the cortical interfaces cross the coupling criterion. If the finest bridge passes P there, equal readouts fit both accounts. If it fails throughout the relevant windows while the unity readout stays intact, P is challenged together with R.

The readout assumption is the same for gradual replacement and for the bridge. Taking unchanged reports as evidence of unchanged unity commits P with R to that challenge. A version of P that lets unity change behind perfectly preserved reports rejects R for those interventions and forfeits this behavioural test. Which package to hold is chosen before the experiment and stays fixed whatever the outcome.

F The occupancy computation

What the membrane is asked. The membrane's next content is the time of its first spike within 10 or 30 ms, and every change of one to 3 noise amplitudes, in either direction, must move that content by the fluctuation. Its time constants span the in vivo high-conductance state and its rates the sparse rates of awake cortex. The passing fractions of Section 3 are for a region that supplies all of the membrane's noise. A bit restored to a rail at the logic node's margin passes at none of its states, and its largest response over them is below 10 -100 . The binary ceiling stays below the fluctuation under every symmetric noise law with one peak that puts less than twice the fluctuation of its mass within one standard deviation of its centre, logistic and Laplace noise included, as shown at the end of this appendix. A graded content clears the fluctuation by a wide margin: at its best state the membrane responds by at least 0.64 in every regime and at every noise share.

Windows.

For independent carriers the chance that none passes within a window falls geometrically with their number: with 100 carriers some carrier passes within 40 ms with probability at least 0.59. Reading the spike time through a clock of 1 or 5 ms leaves the passing fraction unchanged. The value a latch reads links in no window of any length.

Readers that ignore spike times. A reader that registers only whether the membrane fired within the window, and discards every spike time, passes with a next content of 10 ms at the same share of states in every regime as a reader of spike times. At a membrane a few amplitudes below threshold, what a change of one noise amplitude moves is the chance that it fires within the window, and a spike count registers that; a count responds at least as much as this reader, since whether the membrane fired is a function of the count. So P classes a cortical membrane as a graded carrier whether its readers integrate spike times at the grain of milliseconds, as the evidence of Section 2 indicates, or pool spikes over the content's window.

Shared input.

In the barrel cortex of awake mice, the membrane potentials of neighbouring layer 2/3 cells correlate at zero lag by 0.72 on average during quiet wakefulness and by 0.33 while the animal whisks (Poulet & Petersen, 2008). The model gives every membrane a shared component carrying a fraction c of its noise variance, so that two membranes correlate by c and each keeps its own law. At least one of 100 such carriers enters a passing state within 400 ms with probability at least 0.88 for every share up to c = 0.75, in every regime. Both measured correlations lie in that range. The chance of a window without a link grows with the share, so it is at most 0.017 at the whisking correlation and 0.12 at the quiet one. The same recordings show that the input carrying a membrane to its threshold is mostly its own: in the 20 ms before a spike the spiking cell depolarizes by 9 mV and its neighbour by 1.4 mV (Poulet & Petersen, 2008). The model shares that approach in the same proportion as the rest of the fluctuation, so near threshold it correlates the carriers more than the recordings do.

Switching nodes. Take a 1 GHz clock and nodes that switch in 0.02 to 0.5 of its cycles, each transition lasting 20 ps. If a node's next content were the time of its crossing, the node would pass on the rising half of each transition, at 0.02 to 0.5% of its states, within the membrane's range, and within every window of 40 ms except with probability below 10 -100 . By the carrier condition of Section 2, though, a node's next content is what its latch reads at the clock edge, the node at its rail. The crossing a latch discards is exactly the content a membrane delivers when its readers integrate spike times as they arrive. The separation holds for count readers too: a reader that registered only whether a node switched within a cycle would take a quantity fixed by the node's logical inputs, which are restored bits, moved by its noise only through the margin exception probability.

A thalamic relay cell. The integrate-and-fire-or-burst model (Smith et al., 2000), with its published parameters, adds to the membrane a low-threshold calcium current that flows above -60 mV, inactivates there and recovers below it. Noise gives the passive membrane a standard deviation of 2 or 4 mV, the unit of every change. In burst mode a constant current holds the membrane below the calcium threshold, where the current recovers and noise that carries the membrane past the threshold sets off a burst; in tonic mode it holds the membrane above, the current stays inactivated, and the cell is an integrate-and-fire membrane. In each mode the current is calibrated to a rate of 0.5 or 2 Hz, and the next content is the first spike time within 10 or 30 ms, as for the cortical membrane, with the calcium current's state kept under each change. At an instant the two modes pass at similar shares of their states, 0.16 to 1.5% in tonic mode and 0.3 to 1.6% in burst mode. A bursting cell's passing states lie in and around its bursts, which are rare, while a tonic cell's lie below its spike threshold, where it spends the time between spikes. Within 400 ms a tonic cell enters a passing state with probability 0.28 to 0.84, and a bursting cell with probability 0.07 to 0.34. At matched noise, rate and window the tonic cell's chance is at least 2.3 times the bursting cell's, within 40 ms as well. Probability is propagated exactly on a grid in membrane potential and inactivation, and a run at half every grid step moves no visit probability by more than 8.5%.

Recorded membranes. The recordings (Kiritani et al., 2023) hold 240 cells of layers 2/3 to 5 of the barrel cortex of awake head-restrained mice, with quiet wakefulness, free whisking and touch scored from whisker filming; the excitatory cells are the membranes the model describes. Spikes are detected by the authors' criterion for each cell, a cell's threshold is the median potential at spike onset, and each spike, from onset to repolarisation, counts as a failing state, as the model's refractory states do. The awake potential moves on two time scales: fluctuations with a correlation time of 11 to 17 ms, and a wander over hundreds of milliseconds that carries much of its variance. One time constant fitted to both misses the fast fluctuations that set the next spike, so the potential is split into its running mean over 100 ms and a fast remainder. The noise amplitude and the model's time constant are those at which the model membrane, analysed exactly as the recording is, has the remainder's spread and correlation time. Within a next-content window the membrane is taken to be the model membrane with its mean held at the running mean's current value, which supplies the law of the next spike time that a single recorded path does not. Across the 86 cells with at least 10 s of quiet wakefulness, the tenth to ninetieth percentiles run from 2.2 to 5.1 noise amplitudes below threshold, from 0.025 to 1.3% of states passing, with 90% of cells inside the declared range, and from 0.01 to 0.51 for a passing state within 400 ms at a noise share of 1/16; for 31% of cells that chance is below the least declared regime's, 0.085. During free whisking (73 cells) the median cell sits 4.1 amplitudes below threshold and enters a passing state within the window with probability 0.13. Splitting at 200 ms instead gives a median passing share of 0.12% and a median visit probability of 0.13. For the median cell the model predicts 0.47 times the recorded firing rate, and it comes within a factor of two for 48% of cells: recorded membranes fire more readily than a Gaussian membrane at the same distance, and the passing states are read off that Gaussian description. None of the 689 sweeps timed to the second holds two cells recorded at once, so the share of input that neighbouring cells hold in common stays declared.

Figure 2: One protocol at every yardstick. Left: the share of occupied states at which every admissible change moves the next content by at least the yardstick. Right: the chance of entering such a state within 400 ms. The membrane is a band over every declared regime and, on the right, every noise share. A switching node's crossing time is a band over the declared activity factors; it passes exactly at the fluctuation (dotted) and at no higher yardstick. The synchronizer's share is the upper bound T W f D , at the yardsticks one bit can reach, up to Φ(1) -1/2. The value a clocked latch reads passes at no state and in no window.

The yardstick. The separation of the membrane from the value a latch reads holds at every yardstick from 0.01 to 0.6 (Figure 2), not only at the fluctuation. Across that range the latched logic node passes at none of its states, and the membrane enters a passing state within 400 ms with probability at least 0.036 at the highest yardstick, and at least as often at every lower one. Below Φ(1) -1/2 one bit can reach the yardstick, so there a synchronizer's first stage can pass, at no more than 0.2% of its samples. The formal results take the yardstick as a parameter and hold at every value of it. The fluctuation is the natural choice because it makes large mean what it means for the carrier itself: a change that moves the content by as much as the content moves of its own accord.

Method. The membrane is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in units of its own stationary standard deviation, with the threshold at zero. After a spike it is refractory and then reset to its mean, and the mean is calibrated so that the stationary rate equals the declared rate. Probability is propagated on a voltage grid through the exact Ornstein-Uhlenbeck step, and a crossing between two sampled times is counted with the Brownian-bridge probability exp(-2xy/s 2 ) for sub-threshold samples x and y and step deviation s. Nothing is sampled. From each grid state, the law of the first spike time in the window, with its absence as one more outcome, is propagated in one pass, and the response to a change is the total-variation distance between two such laws. A state passes when every admissible change moves the law by at least the fluctuation, where a change is admissible if it is at least one noise amplitude of the carrier and does not carry the membrane across threshold. The fraction of occupied states that pass is the stationary mass of the passing states. The probability of entering a passing state within a window is computed on the same chain with the passing states made absorbing. A carrier that supplies a share φ of the membrane's noise variance has noise amplitude √ φ in the membrane's units, and its changes are scaled accordingly. The bit is a carrier restored each step to a rail at a declared margin, read after one step of unit Gaussian noise, with occupancy given by that noise around the rail. The same computation is repeated at yardsticks from 0.01 to 0.6 in place of the fluctuation, at every regime and noise share. For correlated carriers, each membrane is the sum of a shared Ornstein-Uhlenbeck component of variance c and a private one of variance 1 -c, both with the membrane's time constant. Given the shared path the carriers are independent, so the probability that none of K passes within a window is the average of (1 -h) K over shared paths, where h is one carrier's chance of passing given the path. For each of 256 shared paths from a fixed seed, the membrane's probability is propagated through the exact step with the private noise, its centre moved by the shared path's increment, after a burn-in of five time constants. Halving both the grid spacing and the time step changes the passing fraction by 10%, and the correlation of two carriers' passing by at most 0.012.

Correlation lowers the per-window link. The chance that 100 carriers leave a window of 400 ms without a link is at most 0.0018 at c = 0.25, 0.017 at c = 0.5 and 0.12 at c = 0.75. These bounds, and the links of at least 0.88 and 0.98 in Section 3, lie two Monte Carlo standard errors on the conservative side of the estimate in every regime. The shorter window is more sensitive: within 40 ms the link falls to about 0.23 at c = 0.75, so P's per-window condition is met at the time scale of a percept rather than of its fastest components.

The window is also swept on its own, from one time step to 1000 ms, for independent carriers. The chance that one carrier occupies a passing state at some step of a window is propagated once on the same chain, so every window comes from one pass, and the link of K carriers within it is 1 -(1 -h) K . The link reaches one half in every regime and at every noise share from 3 ms with 1000 carriers and from 31 ms with 100, and since h grows with the window it stays above one half at every longer one. Halving the grid spacing and the time step moves both ends earlier, so these are the conservative values.

The switching chip is counted in closed form. On the rising half of a transition the node's voltage crosses its threshold at a slew V , a change ∆V moves the crossing by ∆V / V and the node's noise jitters it by σ/ V , so the response is 2Φ(∆V /2σ) -1 whatever the slew. Every admissible change of at least one noise amplitude then reaches the fluctuation, exactly at one amplitude, so the node passes at the fluctuation and at no higher yardstick. A node that switches in a fraction α of the cycles of a clock of frequency f , with transitions of duration t, spends αf t/2 of its time on the rising half of one, and a window of N cycles holds no transition with probability (1 -α) N . A synchronizer with aperture T W , clock f C and data changing at rate f D samples inside its aperture at the rate T W f C f D , so at most a share T W f D of its samples do. Each sample is read as one bit, so it passes at no yardstick above Φ(1) -1/2, and at lower yardsticks that share bounds its passing fraction. A second stage allowed a time S to resolve fails on average once every e S/τ /(T W f C f D ) seconds, with τ the stage's resolution time constant (Ginosar, 2011); the declared values are that tutorial's 28 nm example, τ = 10 ps and f D = 100 MHz, with S one cycle.

The one place a working chip latches a transition is a synchronizer between clock domains. With a 20 ps aperture and data changing at 100 MHz (Ginosar, 2011), its first stage samples inside the aperture at most 0.2% of the time, 8 × 10 5 times in a window of 400 ms, and which way it resolves moves with the timing of the transition; a second stage given one cycle to settle leaves it unresolved once in more than 10 29 years. What that second stage takes is the bit the first resolves to. The noise in what the first stage samples includes the transition's own jitter, one amplitude of the change, and it is thermal, so Gaussian, and one bit under Gaussian noise does not reach the fluctuation: at the centre of the aperture, where its two-sided response is largest, a change of one noise amplitude in the transition's timing moves the probability of either resolution by at most Φ(1) -1/2 = 0.34, and the stage's own noise only lowers that. The synchronizer therefore fails graded dependence at every sample, those inside its aperture included, whichever protocol carries the data across the boundary, and so does a random source that reads its bits from how a metastable stage resolves.

The ceiling depends on the noise law only through its mass near the centre. A bit read as 1 when a quantity plus noise exceeds a threshold responds to a change a by the noise law's mass on one of the two intervals of width a that meet at the threshold, so its two-sided response is the smaller of the two, at most half the mass of an interval of width 2a. For a symmetric law with one peak the smaller mass is largest with the threshold at the state, where it is the mass between the centre and one amplitude. One bit therefore stays below the fluctuation at every threshold exactly when the law puts less than twice the fluctuation of its mass within one amplitude of its centre. Scaled to unit standard deviation, Gaussian, logistic and Laplace noise meet this, and a Student law with three degrees of freedom does not.

Several bits held near their thresholds together can read one graded quantity q, as the stages of a time-to-digital converter read one transition time. The word is a function of q plus the quantity's own noise and the stages' noise, and the stages' noise is independent of q. The response of the word to a change of q is therefore at most the response of q itself, 2Φ(a/2σ) -1 under Gaussian noise of amplitude σ, by the data-processing inequality for total variation. With two thresholds half an amplitude on either side of the state and no stage noise, the word's three outcomes split the line where the two laws cross, and a change of one amplitude in either direction moves it by exactly the fluctuation. A word whose thresholds straddle the quantity within its noise thus passes exactly where the quantity passes.

Scope of the estimates. The single-input estimate combines in vitro measurements of one connection type and one noise recording, through a linear threshold crossing. The occupancy computation models one integrate-and-fire membrane under white noise, with a threshold without dynamics of its own, and its time constants, rates, windows, noise shares and carrier counts are declared ranges, not fits. The recorded check covers one area of one species in one dataset without simultaneous recordings, and reads its passing states off a Gaussian model held at the slow part of the potential, which predicts 0.47 times the median cell's firing rate. Correlation is one shared component at declared shares, which span the correlations of neighbouring cells measured in one area of the mouse, and the model shares the approach to threshold in the same proportion, where the recordings show it to be mostly private (Poulet & Petersen, 2008). The carrier counts stay far below the anatomical ones. The per-window bound is proved for independent carriers and, without independence, as the variance of the number that pass over the square of its mean, a ratio that correlation keeps above a floor. The sweep of the window's length assumes independent carriers, and shared input lowers the link most in the shortest windows. The relay cell is a reduced model with no reticular feedback. The passing-state estimates measure candidate sensitivity, not reciprocal contraction of a network's decoded contents. The time windows are declared perceptual scales; the temporal-order threshold supplies a benchmark rather than a universal lower bound on content change.

G Digital hardware in detail

Clockless logic. Asynchronous circuits have no clock. In a quasi-delay-insensitive design, each stage signals completion to the next through a handshake, and correctness holds under every assignment of gate and wire delays apart from a few forks assumed isochronic (Martin & Nyström, 2006).

Their transition times vary gradedly with every voltage, as a spike time does. But the design makes the computed values independent of those times: a value is accepted once its code is complete, whatever delays produced it. The timing of such a circuit is therefore a trace in the sense of Section 2. It moves with the physics, while the circuit's own contents are read from completed codes, each held at a rail by restoring gates, so they meet the margin lemma as a clocked circuit's contents do.

Leakage. Real digital hardware leaks: supply noise, crosstalk and temperature move the analog quantities behind every bit. The margin lemma says where such leakage can reach content. If a content read as a word of thresholded continuous quantities depends gradedly on any region in the exact sense, some bit of the next readout sits on its threshold. Correct sampled operation places those readouts inside margins. Gate restoration stabilizes the rails, and the network of gates supplies logical coordination. The constitutive graph tests whether an admissible physical change inside those margins reaches another content above the yardstick.

The margin also has a width. If every bit of the next state is at least δ from its threshold, each bit is read from an L v -Lipschitz quantity and the micro dynamics is L-Lipschitz, then a change to one region smaller than δ/(LL v ) changes no bit. Leakage below that scale reaches content only through the margin exception probability (Section 3). Above that scale the bound ceases to certify invariance; a sufficiently large disturbance can cause a logical error. Digital design keeps ordinary noise well below that scale: a textbook inverter's static noise margin is 41% of its supply voltage, against an expected supply variation of 10% (Rabaey et al., 2003), so the expected variation is 0.24 of the margin. The nondeterminism of floating-point reduction order is a choice among logical trajectories and lies outside both results: it changes which content is computed, not how content depends on graded state.

The margin's width.

A reliable rail and a near-threshold converter obey different response laws, even on one chip. Adding bits refines the number represented without narrowing any rail's voltage margin. By the noisy margin theorem, reaching the fluctuation with an admissible change inside r/L requires a margin exception probability at least that large. Since that probability counts near approaches to thresholds, it is a different quantity from the processor's logical error rate, and the criterion is applied to each physical readout over its actual input range. The examples compare rails 506 noise amplitudes from threshold with model membranes averaging 2.0 to 3.5 amplitudes below it.

A converter driven by an external graded signal is judged with that signal's noise and its reader's integration time, and a word of bits or repeated measurements may carry a graded response at that scale. For a hybrid system the question is which such carriers overlap, and whether their responses and restoration meet P in every content window.

Scope of the hardware examples.

The margin exception probability counts near approaches as well as errors, so it is generally larger than a logical error rate. The single-bit ceiling holds for the stated symmetric single-peaked noise laws; a Student law with three degrees of freedom can break it. A word of bits read jointly, or a sequence integrated over time, needs its own response law. The thermal and switching examples declare their capacitance, clock, activity, transition time and synchronizer.

H The bridge in detail

Instantaneous design estimates. For an additive Gaussian channel, at unit gain, an input shift of one source noise amplitude reaches the fluctuation when the effective channel noise is at most that amplitude. These quantities are evaluated at the chosen input and output coordinates, after filtering. A scalar quantizer suppresses a change at states sufficiently far from an edge. With the declared noise, being farther than the source's noise plus 0.3 times the recording noise suffices for one admissible perturbation to miss the yardstick.

Under the information-matching approximation in the estimate, matching by adding noise to the analog channel would require noise of standard deviation 0.24 times the quantizer's step. Keeping that channel sensitive then caps the step at 4.1 source noise amplitudes. Under uniform occupancy within a step, the resulting fraction of states certified to fail is at most 52%. Lowering bandwidth instead preserves this instantaneous noise budget while changing the time course. The reported step of 10 noise amplitudes, with the declared recording noise, gives a certified failing fraction of at least 74% under the same occupancy assumption.

A first-order filter of cutoff f c has time constant 1/(2πf c ). The design floor of 1 Hz compares this constant with the restoration deadline in Appendix B. The preparation also measures total delay and the closed loop's recovery of disagreement. The filter floor is a preliminary constraint; meeting the deadline is a property of the whole loop. Settings are fixed once the information controls are met and each arm's temporal classification is established, and before any outcome is compared.

The complete reader and the content window. For a micro state x, let C next j be the next content actually taken from carrier j, including any integration of several samples by its reader. Let A i (x) contain the admissible changes of source carrier i, between its noise and its threshold, with other coordinates fixed. Write

The laws are interventional, using the same declared noise process in each case. An empty A i (x) is excluded from certification. For a trajectory X and a content window T , define

This expresses the carrier and window criterion used in Section 3. Both directions are evaluated, and the probability that both occur in the same window is estimated with their dependence retained.

Restoring dynamics and its deadline are checked by a separate perturbation of overlap discrepancy.

The order of quantifiers matters. The instantaneous failing fraction measures time spent outside the passing set, whereas G ab records whether the set is visited at all, and a brief approach to threshold is enough to set it to one. Several thresholds reading the same graded input can also preserve information that a single bit loses, as the example in Appendix F shows. A reader that integrates successive symbols is assessed on that joint sequence: repeated noisy observations can resolve an input change that a single observation misses. Filter memory, timing of code changes, recording noise correlations and downstream membrane integration belong in this next-readout law.

To exclude a route by the noisy margin theorem, apply it to the full map from the perturbed state to this next readout. Its Lipschitz constant and exception probability cover the whole map and all relevant samples, and an admissible change must remain inside its effective margin. A singlesample margin bound provides that certificate only when the next readout uses that sample alone.

To establish a passing route, lower confidence bounds must cover every admissible change for a selected carrier pair; a finite grid needs justified monotonicity or regularity between its points. To establish failure, an upper bound below the yardstick for one admissible change suffices for each candidate pair, at every state the window visits. The observation window, intervention duration and tolerances are fixed before outcome comparisons. The preparation measures alternative anatomical routes as part of the same audit.

A specified dynamical alternative. Let z t contain the recurrent observer's estimates of the locations carried by the two regions. At the chosen sampling interval its pilot-fitted update is where ℓ t is local sensory evidence, u t is the delivered bridge signal, d is its measured delay, and ξ t has the calibrated residual law.

The recorded input passes through the measured filters and, in the quantized arm, the quantizer before entering u t . Parameters describing the cortical observer are shared across arms; the measured circuit transformation changes with bandwidth and resolution. The state includes filter and delay memory.

For the matching task let m t = w ⊤ z t be the predicted difference of the two location estimates. If the decision is same when |m t + e t | ≤ r, the model's choice probability is with F e the pilot-fitted continuous cumulative distribution of decision noise and a fixed criterion r.

For unity reports the specified alternative is where v t is the observer's uncertainty about the location difference and q t is the independently measured local visibility score.

The coefficients are fitted on calibration blocks and fixed for the comparison. Both decision models use a common rule across arms, with no free coefficient for the analog or quantized label.

Calibrating the report readout. Before the human bridge comparison, the same subject performs a separate calibration with the natural connection intact. The two fields carry distinguishable features, presented together on some trials and in deliberate alternation at several dwell times on others. Where an ambiguous display elicits reported perceptual switches, it provides a further timing control: alternation of the stimuli is not assumed to equal alternation of experience. A cue at an unpredictable time asks whether the features were present in one simultaneous scene at that instant, appeared in succession, or only one was present; "uncertain" is an available answer. Other trials probe each feature separately, to measure local visibility and report ability without requiring a judgment of unity. Report category, latency and confidence are recorded, with continuous switch reports in designated calibration blocks. Eye position and intracranial activity constrain the timing and local availability of the features. A decoder trained on local-feature trials is held fixed across conditions; concurrent neural decoding is not itself a measure of experienced unity. An optional functional MRI localizer can be collected in a separate session; the bridge comparison uses the intracranial recordings and reports from the same trials.

The report analysis compares two fitted accounts. A joint-state account permits both features in one candidate perceptual state. A switching account has states in which one field or the other is current, with fitted dwell times, memory and report integration; it can therefore predict an answer of "one scene" even after a succession of separate states. Both accounts take the observer's estimated feature states as input and share measured local visibility, task evidence, report delays and decision biases. The logistic p U above is the observer's marginal prediction for the unity answer; the report models extend it to the distribution of report category, latency, confidence and local-probe answers. Calibration fits those distributions and scores both accounts on held-out trials. The report criterion, temporal range, minimum held-out separation between their predicted distributions and equivalence margins for local visibility and report ability are fixed from pilot data before bridge outcomes are examined. Fitted report parameters are then frozen; the measured bridge signals may change the models' inputs but the arm label adds no free report parameter.

The human comparison is informative about R only in blocks where the calibrated models make separable report predictions, both fields remain locally available, and the physical test classifies the bridge routes. The primary report contrast is the probability of a simultaneous-scene answer after the unpredictable cue, with local-feature detection and report ability matched across arms. Latency, confidence and switch reports test the switching account on held-out blocks. The recurrent observer is scored against the full report distribution, not just the fraction of simultaneous answers. If switching is faster than the calibrated report and neural resolution, or if the two fitted accounts make equivalent predictions, these observations do not distinguish switching from unity. The calibration tests the usefulness of R at the measured time scale; it does not turn reports or coactive neural signals into direct observations of experience.

The factorial comparison fits the effects of bandwidth and quantization separately, while the resolution sweep at fixed bandwidth tests their interaction with noise and delay. The experiment records impulse responses, output spectra, stimulation gain and discrepancy recovery as well as transfer entropy and task information. Predictions concern the complete response and recovery distributions on held-out blocks. This alternative can predict an analog advantage from smoothing or a quantized advantage from transmitted signal strength. P with R additionally rules out preserved unity reports in a condition certified to fail its coupling requirement. A condition that both accounts predict alike measures their common mechanism; a disagreement between their predictions defines the decisive comparison.

Whether the loops can be matched. The saved simulations assess information matching for transmission from region A to region B, at a 1 ms step and in units of A's noise amplitude. The proposed preparation uses reciprocal loops and adds the temporal certification and observer comparison above. A task variable, a process of standard deviation 2 to 10 and time constant 20 or 100 ms, drives region A on top of A's own noise. A is recorded with noise of its own amplitude and passed through the shared filter, then through the analog loop's cutoff or the quantizer, and the shared output stage drives region B, a leaky integrator with noise of its own. Both quantities are estimated twice. The linear estimator takes transfer entropy from A's recording to B's by the linear-Gaussian formula, and task decodability as the variance of the task variable that a linear decoder of B's recording explains on held-out trials. It misses what the quantizer's nonlinearity passes on, so the nearest-neighbour estimator takes transfer entropy as a conditional mutual information (Kraskov et al., 2004; Frenzel & Pompe, 2007) and decodability as the variance a decoder would explain if the task information in B's recording, estimated the same way, were Gaussian; on the analog loop the two estimators agree. For each step and estimator, two cutoffs are read off a grid from the floor above to 1 kHz: the one that matches the quantized loop's transfer entropy and the one that matches its decodability. Both measures rise with the cutoff, so at the lower of the two the analog loop carries no more of either.

At the step of 10 noise amplitudes, in every regime whose task variable spans at least half a step, the linear transfer entropy is matched between 17 and 95 Hz, well above the floor, and the matched analog loop explains 0.025 to 0.06 less of the task variable's variance than the quantized loop.

The same holds at every simulated step no larger than twice the task variable's standard deviation.

Lowering the bandwidth removes fast activity that carries transfer entropy and little of the task, while the quantizer removes small changes at every frequency, so at matched linear transfer entropy the quantized loop keeps more of the task. When the task variable spans only a fifth of a step, the matched analog loop can carry more task information, by up to 0.075, and the step has to be made finer before the loops are compared. The task is therefore chosen so that its variable spans several noise amplitudes of the recorded region.

By the nearest-neighbour estimator the quantized loop carries more transfer entropy than the analog loop does at any cutoff up to 1 kHz, because its jumps tell the driven region when the recorded one crossed a step, so at the declared step no cutoff matches it. At the steps where one does, the matched analog loop carries more task information in 4 of 7 cases, by up to 0.038: which side of a transfer-entropy match the task information falls on depends on the estimator. The lower match does not. The nearest-neighbour decodability is matched between 33 and 399 Hz, above the linear transfer-entropy match in every regime, so the lower match is the linear one, and a preparation sets the cutoff there. At that cutoff, by the nearest-neighbour estimator, the analog loop carries 10 to 55% less transfer entropy and explains 0.028 to 0.065 less of the task variable's variance than the quantized loop, and it carries less of both at every simulated step no larger than twice the task variable's standard deviation.

On the preparation, the decoder is fitted on other blocks of the same loop, the step and the cutoff are set together on pilot blocks, and the check is repeated on the blocks that are compared.

Certifying failure over a window. Criterion G passes a loop whose quantizer input visits a passing state anywhere in a content window, and a continuous task variable crosses the quantizer's edges as it moves. At the declared step, in every simulated regime whose task variable spans half a step, the quantized loop's input came within the passing distance of an edge in 100% of the simulated 400 ms windows. With such a task both loops pass P, and the decisive blocks do not arise. The task therefore presents one stimulus per trial, held for the trial, whose represented value lies within 0.5 noise amplitudes of the centre of a step. With 3 or 5 such stimuli, the simulated input visited the passing band in at most 21% of windows, and the quantized loop is certified to fail in the rest. A change of stimulus crosses an edge, so the window is the period in which the content is held, after the loop has settled at the new level: in simulation it opens 5 time constants of the slowest analog filter after the stimulus. Held stimuli also give a comparison within the quantized arm. The loop records its own input, so its trials divide into those whose input visited the passing band and those whose input stayed clear of it, and P with R predicts that the second lose the calibrated unity readout more often than the first. A visit also marks a larger excursion of noise, so the recurrent observer is scored on the same division.

With held stimuli both loops deliver the stimulus almost completely: a linear decoder of B's recording explains at least 0.99 of its variance, for the quantized loop and for the analog loop at its slowest cutoff, 1 Hz. Most of the transfer entropy then comes from the held level, and at that cutoff the analog loop carries 107 to 108% of the quantized loop's linear transfer entropy, so lowering its bandwidth cannot match the pair. The analog loop therefore adds white noise of its own before its cutoff filter. The filter passes little of that noise to the delivered current, where the loop still passes while its noise stays within one noise amplitude of the region, as in the instantaneous estimate above. The pilot blocks set the noise at which the analog loop carries 5% less linear transfer entropy than the quantized loop and no more task information. In simulation that noise is 9.4 noise amplitudes, and the loop's noise at the delivered current, filtered recording noise included, is 0.53 amplitudes. On 16 further blocks of 100 trials, the analog loop then carries at most 97% of the quantized loop's linear transfer entropy in every held regime, and no more task information. At these rates the nearest-neighbour estimate of transfer entropy is dominated by its bias, so the linear estimate sets this match.

With blocks of 100 trials repeated on independent noise, the matched transfer entropy and the gap vary from block to block, and their confidence intervals narrow with the square root of the trials. The behavioural comparison, accuracy 0.75 against 0.7 at a two-sided level of 0.05 and power 0.8, needs 1248 trials per loop, and the neural comparison, at a standardized difference of 0.2, needs 393. At the behavioural count, by either estimator, the model's transfer entropies are estimated to within 4.4% and the difference in task variance to within 0.006, smaller than every margin above in these simulations. Those counts describe the declared pairwise effects. Pilot data determine the repeatedblock variance, multiple-comparison plan and equivalence power for the factorial experiment and report readout. The limits of this transmission model are collected in Section 8.

The analog arm is kept analog end to end so that quantization is an explicit experimental factor. Each arm's status under P is determined by the complete response protocol above.

Stimulation artefact. Event-triggered loops blank the recording around each pulse, and a continuous drive leaves no interval to blank. The loops therefore record and stimulate in separate frequency bands. Each loop reads multi-unit activity, above a few hundred hertz, takes its envelope, and drives the other region with a current that follows the envelope and so lies in the band below it. Rectifying and smoothing are analog operations, so the analog loop stays analog end to end. What leaks across the bands is removed by subtracting the loop's own output, which the loop knows exactly, passed through the transfer from stimulator to recording contact measured on open-loop calibration blocks. Both loops end in the same output stage, which smooths the quantizer's steps into the stimulation band, and share the stimulator, the bands and the subtraction, so both arms use the same artefact path. Their different waveforms can still produce different residuals. Open-loop blocks in which each stimulator follows activity recorded in another block estimate that residual separately in every bandwidth and quantization condition. Its uncertainty is propagated to the response bounds and the outcome comparison.

Writing a location across a population.

A location is carried by a population whose units have receptive fields, and one current cannot write it. The bridge therefore runs one loop per channel: each recording channel in A is paired with the stimulating channel in B whose units share its receptive field, so the delivered pattern is topographic, and each quantized channel has its own quantizer. Simultaneous stimulation through many electrodes in visual cortex already produces percepts of shapes, motion and letters matched to the electrodes' receptive fields (Chen et al., 2020). Microstimulation activates a sparse and distributed set of neurons, partly through their axons, rather than a dense volume around the tip (Histed et al., 2009), so the transfer from each stimulating channel to B's population is measured on open-loop blocks, and the task variable is the one decoded from the activity each loop evokes in B. Both arms share the channel map, the stimulator and that transfer.

The simulations above model one channel.

Interrupting the connection. The natural route is interrupted at its terminals. Projection neurons in A express an inhibitory designer receptor targeted to their axons, and its ligand, delivered locally in B, suppresses their release there, reversibly and only on that pathway (Stachniak et al., 2014). Optogenetic inhibition at terminals attenuates evoked release when timed precisely, while sustained archaerhodopsin activation increases spontaneous release (Mahn et al., 2016), so it suits only brief blocks. Indirect routes, through the pulvinar or other cortical areas, remain, so the natural route is reduced rather than severed. The directed perturbations measure how much of a nudge in A still reaches B with both loops off, and that residual enters the certification as a biological path of its own. It is measured before and after every block, because it can grow: behaviour impaired by acute silencing of an area recovers spontaneously within days of a permanent lesion of the same area (Otchy et al., 2015), and a pathway silenced for weeks invites the same compensation. A ceiling on the residual, fixed before any comparison, is the largest residual at which the quantized loop's complete map to B, residual path included, still fails criterion G; a block in which the ceiling is crossed leaves the quantized arm uncertified.

A preparation that changes over weeks. A bridge experiment runs for weeks, and the substrate it tests changes with it. Unbridged blocks interleaved with bridged ones in every session give a sameday baseline, so recovery through other routes is subtracted session by session rather than once per animal. The bridge is itself a plasticity protocol: the spike-triggered implant cited as precedent reorganized motor cortex output over days, with changes lasting more than a week (Jackson et al., 2006), and the two arms deliver different waveforms and may induce different changes. The recommended design counterbalances the order of the arms across animals and runs the fewest sessions the power analysis allows. Acute preparations remove both processes at a cost in trials per animal, and are the alternative for a first arm; the choice rests on pilot variance and belongs to the experiment.

Learned stimulation codes.

A stable stimulation pattern can be learned as a symbol: monkeys learn to discriminate objects signalled only by temporal patterns of intracortical microstimulation (O'Doherty et al., 2011). A quantized loop whose levels stay fixed for weeks could restore behavioural integration through a learned code rather than through coupling, and that would read as a preserved readout in a condition certified to fail P. Two signatures separate the routes. A readout restored by coupling is present from the first bridged blocks, while one restored by a learned code improves over sessions, so the readout is reported session by session as well as pooled. And a learned code is tied to the levels it was learned on. The recommended control relabels the loop between sessions: the held stimuli and the quantizer's levels shift together by a fraction of a step, a half step in the simulations, in both arms. Every stage of the model loop other than the quantizer is linear and time-invariant, and the quantizer commutes with the joint shift, so every signal moves by a constant. In simulation the quantized loop's transfer entropy and task information, by both estimators, and its visits to the passing band are unchanged, and every level it delivers is one the unshifted sessions never delivered. The stimuli stay at the centres of steps, so the certification stands.

A readout that rests on how B's own dynamics read the delivered current follows the shift, since A's stimulus and B's current move together; a code learned on the earlier sessions' levels does not.

A learned code that interpolates between levels can survive the shift, and the time course is what catches it. Permuting the levels instead breaks every learned map, and also breaks the topographic correspondence through which B reads the current, so a readout lost under permutation does not tell the two routes apart. Which relabelling a preparation uses, and how often, is a choice for the experiment.

Size of the experiment. The trial counts above are per loop condition. They multiply with the cells of the factorial design and the blocks of the resolution sweep, and they grow with the equivalence margins that preserved reports need. The number of cells is therefore fixed from pilot variance, before any comparison, and a first experiment can run the information-controlled pair and its unbridged control before the full factorial.

Scope of the simulations.

The saved simulations show that information can be controlled in a one-directional transmission model with declared noise and filters.

They do not establish that the full reciprocal preparation falls on opposite sides of P, and they do not fit the rival observer. The model has no spikes, stimulation artefact or plasticity. Over the weeks an experiment runs, indirect routes can strengthen and the bridge can reorganize the connections it drives; the design measures the residual route in every block and bounds it in advance, and does not model either process. Relabelling leaves the information a loop carries unchanged exactly in the linear model only, and on a preparation it is measured on the relabelled blocks. The fraction of time a loop fails at an instant does not certify that it fails over a whole window, and bounds on single bits do not certify a reader of a joint word or of repeated samples. Temporal response, alternative anatomical routes and restoration need measuring. The factorial comparison and resolution sweep are proposals, with power and equivalence margins to be set on pilot data.

I Timing the field's cone

Brain tissue carries an electric field as well as synapses. At the frequencies of neural activity that field is quasi-static (Gratiy et al., 2017): it reaches every point of the tissue it spans with a propagation delay negligible on the neural time scales considered here. Synaptic influence between distant regions, by contrast, arrives only after axonal conduction and synaptic transmission, no sooner than 8 ms across the longest cortico-cortical fibres. If two regions re-agree after a local perturbation faster than the synaptic route allows, the coupling has a non-synaptic part, and the timing measures the reach of the kernel tail of Section 4 directly.

The field's strength sets the distance at which the test of the field's causal cone in Section 6 can decide anything. Endogenous fields in cortex peak near 2.4 mV/mm in vivo (Fröhlich & McCormick, 2010), networks of neurons detect fields from 0.14 mV/mm (Francis et al., 2003), and the potential of a local cortical source decays as r -2.1 across millimetres (Rebollo et al., 2021). With the peak placed at the nearest distance of that measurement, the field of a local source falls to the detection threshold within 3.8 mm, and misses it by 5 orders of magnitude at 15 cm and by 3.5 at 5 cm. The field's cone is therefore tested at millimetre distances, where activity has been observed to synchronize across a cut through cortex by the field alone (Rebollo et al., 2021). At centimetre distances P predicts that re-agreement arrives through synaptic coupling, which is graded as well.

The timing can be measured with intracortical recording, with care. The stimulation artefact saturates clinical amplifiers during the first milliseconds, masking the earliest monosynaptic responses (Keller et al., 2014), and early responses at distant contacts carry a volume-conducted component that scales with distance as the artefact does (Prime et al., 2020). Three measures separate active re-agreement from the passive field that carries the stimulus: template subtraction of the artefact (Trebaul et al., 2016); multi-unit activity or current-source density at the distant site, which the passive spread of the local field potential does not reach (Kajikawa & Schroeder, 2011); and a deadline set for each subject from the tractography length of the connecting fibres (Caminiti et al., 2013).

Scope. A long-range tail improves agreement only in proportion to its conductance against the short-range part. The field's reach rests on an estimate that places its peak at a declared distance, and its contribution across centimetres is a quantity to be measured.

J Further related work

Embodied architectures. Starzyk & Galus (2026) propose that candidate conditions for consciousness involve sensory representations integrated with regulation, affect and recurrent feedback in the Motivated Emotional Mind (MEM) architecture, and leave realization in artificial substrates as a hypothesis to be tested through causal organization and temporal dynamics. P gives one part of that question, the coupling of contents, a mechanistic criterion: whether their carriers respond gradedly above noise and restore agreement within a content window, measured by the same intervention on any substrate. MEM's call for comparisons with competing architectures and hybrids is the kind of explicit model comparison the bridge builds in.

Biology and the medium. Seth (2026) argues that consciousness may depend on biological properties that computation does not capture. P makes one such property explicit, and measurable: sensitivity above noise and restoration within a window, assessed by one protocol on membranes and logic nodes. It locates that property in how the substrate is organised, and admits non-biological hardware that has it (Section 5). Mortal computation, whose parameters are useful only on the hardware instance that learned them (Hinton, 2022; Ororbia & Friston, 2023), shares P's refusal to separate the computation from the medium.

The distinction also concerns where a learning signal is available. Under the noisy-margin hypotheses a content read from bits has a response no larger than its margin exception probability (Section 3; Appendix K); a graded substrate can carry a local response to a weak nudge as it relaxes. Weak nudges followed by relaxation are also used in equilibrium propagation (Scellier & Bengio, 2017), while physical networks can be trained with a hybrid physical and digital backpropagation procedure (Wright et al., 2022). P supplies neither a learning rule nor an advantage in learning or representation: digital hardware can retain smaller changes by using more bits, and the reach bound in Section 4 expresses consistency across a distributed content.

Analog and digital. On the mechanistic account of Piccinini (2008), a digital computer manipulates strings of digits, states its components distinguish reliably, and which class a system belongs to is fixed by its mechanism. P's symbol, a content read through a noise margin, is that reliability stated as a property of the readout, with the margin measured in the parts' own noise; P then asks what the reliability costs, namely graded dependence below the margin. Maley (2011) separates analog from continuous and digital from discrete representation, and P's line follows the second pair, not the first: a spike time is a physical content whether or not it represents by analogy, and a continuous quantity latched through a margin is a symbol. Maudlin (1989) argues that a computation's counterfactual structure can be carried by machinery that is idle on the actual run, which sits badly with consciousness supervening on present physical activity. P states its counterfactual condition on present activity: graded dependence asks how the actual carriers respond to changes of the actual state, above their noise, and idle machinery responds to none.

Field theories. The electromagnetic field theory of McFadden (2020) identifies consciousness with the brain's field, supported by evidence that endogenous fields entrain cortical activity (Fröhlich & McCormick, 2010). Miller et al. (2026) place cognition and consciousness in travelling waves that synaptic and ephaptic coupling sustain together, and take consciousness to arise when those waves bring cortex into a globally integrated state. Their analog computation is set apart from digital computation by running in parallel. P treats the field, and the waves it carries, as ways among several to realize graded coupling, and draws the line between analog and digital at the noise margin, which a parallel digital machine keeps.
